title: Effect of aging temperature on the microstructure and tribological behavior of an 18Ni maraging steel manufactured by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)
abstract: Abstract This study addresses the critical knowledge gap regarding the influence of kinetically controlled austenite reversion on the tribological stability of Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) 18Ni-300 maraging steel. While conventional aging focuses on peak hardness (450–550 °C), this research investigates the high-temperature aging regime (610 °C and 650 °C) to elucidate the correlation between phase meta-stability and the evolution of protective tribo-layers. Samples were characterized using LOM, SEM, and XRD, with wear performance evaluated via pin-on-disk testing. A significant novelty of this work is the identification of a trevorite-rich oxide layer (Ni 0.86 Fe 2+ 0.12 Co 0.01 )Fe 3+ 2 O 4  whose formation is directly promoted by the presence of reverted austenite. In contrast, hematite was found to form predominantly on the martensitic substrate. Results show that prolonging aging at 610 °C from 10 to 30 min reduced hardness from 540 HV 0.2  to 511 HV 0.2  due to precipitate coarsening and increased austenite reversion. Although high-temperature aging enhances wear resistance compared to the as-built state, the higher austenite content at 610 °C facilitated oxide layer detachment, increasing the coefficient of friction (CoF) to 0.58, compared to 0.44 observed at 650 °C. These findings provide a technical basis for optimizing 3D-printed components, shifting the focus from maximum hardness to the engineering of phase-stabilized tribological surfaces.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Maraging steels are ultra-high-strength iron-based alloys primarily alloyed with Ni, Co, and Mo. Since their development in the late 1950s [ 1 ], these materials have evolved significantly, progressing from the 200 ksi series to the 450 series, achieving strengths near 3000 MPa [ 2 ,  3 ]. Due to their exceptional mechanical profile, they are indispensable in the aerospace, nuclear, and high-performance tooling industries [ 4 ,  5 ]. Recently, Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) has expanded their application to complex 3D-printed components. 18Ni Maraging 300 steel is a premier candidate for LPBF due to its superior printability and dimensional stability [ 6 ]. Unlike conventional processing, LPBF-fabricated steels exhibit highly segregated microstructures that allow for precise tailoring of properties via post-processing heat treatments [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ].

The strength of 18Ni maraging steel stems from its low-carbon martensitic matrix, further enhanced by precipitation hardening during aging (typically 450–550 °C). In this stage, nanometric intermetallics such as Ni 3 Ti, Ni 3 Mo, Fe 2 Mo nucleate within the matrix [ 3 ,  10 ]. However, elevating temperatures or extending durations triggers particle coarsening and the diffusion-controlled reversion of martensite into austenite [ 10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ]. While reverted austenite can improve the strength-ductility balance through the Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) effect and crack propagation resistance, excessive formation eventually compromises hardness. This microstructural evolution is governed by complex kinetics.

In LPBF materials, the high cooling rates and spatial thermal gradients modulate nucleation and growth kinetics, inducing significant heterogeneities. Consequently, understanding the impact of heat treatments on mechanical and wear resistance is essential for industrial optimization [ 17 ]. For instance, while aging LPBF 18Ni-300 steel at 480 °C can increase UTS from 1231 MPa to 2133 MPa, it significantly reduces elongation [ 9 ]. Such trade-offs necessitate a strategic selection of parameters to meet specific application requirements [ 18 ,  19 – 20 ]. Recent research has begun to explore the tribological behavior of AM maraging steels. Tonolini et al. [ 21 ] demonstrated that direct aging of AM samples could match the performance of conventionally processed materials, potentially reducing processing time. However, literature regarding wear under overaging conditions remains limited. Podgornik et al. [ 17 ] observed that annealed and aged samples exhibited inferior wear resistance compared to directly aged material. Bae et al. [ 22 ] identified a load-dependent response, where heat treatment benefits diminished as wear loads escalated from 5 N to 50 N. Furthermore, Yin et al. [ 23 ] highlighted that phase transformations are more sensitive to temperature than time, noting a transition from abrasive wear in the as-built state to the formation of adhesive tribofilms in the aged state due to increased hardness and reverted austenite.

Despite these studies, a gap remains in understanding how kinetically controlled austenite reversion—specifically above standard aging (> 550 °C) ranges—affects the stability of protective oxide layers during sliding and impact the wear behavior of the 18Ni steel. This study investigates the impact of high-temperature aging (610 °C and 650 °C) on the wear mechanisms of LPBF 18Ni-300 maraging steel. By correlating microstructural states with the evolution of specific tribo-oxides, such as NiFe₂O₄ trevorite spinel and hematite, this research provides a technical basis for optimizing components subjected to wear environments.

sections.heading: Sample preparation and chemical composition
paragraphs: Samples of maraging steel were manufactured by LPBF technique using a metal 3D printer EOS M280. The processing parameters consisted of a 180 W laser power, 100 μm beam diameter, 900 mm·s⁻¹ scanning speed, a layer thickness of 50 μm, using and strategy of 67° rotation between layers. EOS GmbH supplied the powder with the respective chemical composition measured by X-ray fluorescence (18.27Ni, 8.67Co, 5.57Mo, 0.73Ti, and Fe-balance (wt%). 55 wear test samples were fabricated shown in Fig.  1 a, all parallel to the build axis, achieving 99.19% density [ 24 ].

The as-built (AB) samples were subjected to heat treatments (aging) to study the evolution of austenite phase transformation and its influence on wear and friction behavior, without any prior heat treatment to solubilize or relieve stress. Many studies report enhanced reversion from 600 to 700 °C during shorter periods of heat-treatment [ 12 ,  25 ]. This was in accordance with previous data that we collected with in-situ gradual austenite reversion. The specific heat treatments were selected to study samples with and without reverted austenite to evaluate the effect of this phase on wear. The applied heat treatments consisted of isothermal treatment of 610 °C for 10 min, 610 °C for 30 min, and 650 °C for 10 min. Table  1  summarizes the heat treatment conditions analyzed in this study. AB represents the As-built material, 610 − 10 is the material aged at 610 °C for 10 min, 610 − 30 is the sample treated at 610 °C for 30 min, and 650 − 10 is the sample treated at 650 °C for 10 min. These aging temperatures (610 °C and 650 °C for 10–30 min) were selected to investigate the tribological performance because promote diffusion-controlled transformation of martensite into austenite unlike standard aging at 480 °C. The experimental matrix was designed to evaluate distinct overaging mechanisms: 610 °C / 10 min targets austenite stabilization via Ni-partitioning; 610 °C / 30 min investigates time-dependent overaging and phase growth; and 650 °C / 10 min explores temperature-induced overaging and phase instability due to Ni-dilution. This approach enables a direct correlation between matrix stability and the nucleation of protective tribo-oxides, such as NiFe₂O₄ trevorite spinel.

In practice, aging heat treatment aims to optimize precipitation in terms of size and dispersion. However, the present heat treatment applied does not seek to optimize precipitation, but rather to induce austenite reversion, which in some cases induces coarse precipitation. This is generally called tempering. Nonetheless, the studied heat treatment shall be called aging in the entire manuscript.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs: To reveal the different aspects of microstructural characterization, the samples were prepared using conventional metallographic techniques, i.e., grinding from 80 to 1200 mesh with SiC paper followed by polishing with a diamond paste of 6, 3, and 1 μm and finally, the samples were etched with 2% Nital (2% HNO₃ in ethanol) for 10 s. Then, the samples were investigated by Light Optical Microscopy (LOM) (Nikon Epiphot 200) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) (JEOL JSM 6490-LV) coupled with Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX) (Oxford IncaPentaFETx-3). X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed using an X’Pert PRO diffractometer with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15418 nm) in a Bragg-Brentano configuration. The measurements were conducted over an angular range (2θ) from 15° to 80°, employing a step size of 0.05° and a counting time of 2.0 s per step, operating at 45 kV and 30 mA. Phase quantification was performed using the Rietveld refinement method and software known as Material Analysis Using Diffraction (MAUD). The Rietveld refinement process utilizes a least-squares minimization algorithm, in which the discrepancies between the observed experimental data and the simulated diffraction profile are squared, weighted, and summed. The characteristics of the simulated profile are governed by the active parameters and how their values reduce the difference between the experimental data and the calculated pattern. Multiple refinement cycles are typically performed to further optimize these parameters and enhance the fit between the model and the experimental results.

sections.heading: Hardness
paragraphs: Measurement of hardness was performed according to the ASTM E384-17 standard. The Vickers indentation was carried out on micro-scale, with a 200 g load and 15 s dwell time using a Computer-Assisted Microhardness System (Shimadzu Micro Vickers Hardness Tester HMV-G 21 series).

sections.heading: Tribological tests
paragraphs: Tribological tests were conducted in a pin-on-disk tribometer as shown in Fig.  1 b, in dry sliding conditions at room conditions (temperature ≈ 26 °C, relative humidity ≈ 67%), according to parameters shown in Table  3 . The counter bodies were spheres of 6 mm in diameter of WC-Co (manufactured by Goodfellow), which were in contact with a block specimen of 20 mm in length, 10 of width and 8 in thickness, Fig.  1 c. At least three tests were conducted to guarantee statistical representativity, with the sliding test occurring on the build plane (i.e., plane perpendicular to the build direction).

Fig. 1 ( a ) Picture from maraging build after PBF fabrication; ( b ) Pin on disk tribometer; ( c ) Samples of 18Ni maraging steel manufactured by Laser Melting Powder Bed Fusion technology. Samples were subjected to wear testing on the build plane. BD: build direction; TD: transverse direction

A cleaning step was conducted before and after tribological testing, which consisted of immersing the specimens for 10 min in an ethanol bath assisted by ultrasound and drying with compressed clean air. In this step, loose debris was removed from the surfaces of both specimens, and the mass was later measured using a precision balance (10 − 4  mg of resolution) Mettler Toledo MX5 to determine the tribological performance of the studied systems. In addition, the surface of the wear tracks of each disk specimen were investigated by LOM and SEM coupled with EDX for elemental compositional microanalysis. To analyze the effect of oxide formation during the sliding tests in the friction response, Raman analyses were conducted in a HORIBA JOBIN YVON (Labram HR model) high-resolution confocal Raman micro-spectroscope with a helium-neon laser with 633 nm, using an arrangement of 42 by 26 points (1,092 measurements) with steps of 0.4 μm and acquisition time of 1 s.
Table 3 Parameters for tribological tests Parameter Value Load [N] 5 Sliding velocity [mm/s] 10 Sliding distance [m] 200 Track diameter [mm] 4 Diameter counter body [mm] 6

The coefficient of friction (CoF) was measured directly on the pin on the disk tribometer. The wear rate  WR  [kg/Nm] was determined by the mass loss Δ m  after tribological test [kg], divided by the normal load applied  L  [N], and the sliding distance  d  [m] on the test using equation, assuming no significant pin wear. Usually, ASTM G133 [ 26 ] presents wear rate as mm³/mm or mm³/s. But normalizing this wear rate by the applied load became something interesting and desirable due to Archard’s deduction that the wear rate is proportional to the applied load [ 27 ]. Therefore, what is called the specific wear rate can then be expressed per [mm³/Nm] [ 28 ], which can also be [kg/Nm].

The values of the coefficient of friction and wear rate were obtained after three tests for each condition As-Built, 610 °C–10 min, 610 °C–30 min and 650 °C–10 min, using the mean and standard deviation of experimental tests.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs: Figure  2 a presents LOM images of the 18Ni maraging steel sample in the as-built condition. The microstructure observed on the build plane (see Fig.  3 b) reveals the characteristic laser track pattern. Figure  2 b–d, on the other hand, show samples subjected to aging treatments, displaying typical lath martensitic microstructures. Notably, in the sample aged at 610 °C for 10 min, the outlines of laser track are still visible. On the other hand, the sample aged at 610 °C for 30 min exhibits a strong etching response, suggesting the highest density or coalescence of precipitated secondary phases due more treatment time. For the sample aged at 650 °C for 10 min (Fig.  2 d), the microstructure shows an advanced stage of matrix homogenization; the higher thermal energy provided at this temperature facilitates the dissolution of the cell-like solidification structure, resulting in a more uniform lath martensitic distribution with nearly indistinguishable melt pool boundaries.

Fig. 2 Light optical microscopy images of 18Ni maraging steel in the ( a ) as-built condition, and after aging at ( b ) 610 °C for 10 min, ( c ) 610 °C for 30 min, and ( d ) 650 °C for 10 min. Images obtained on the build plane

Figure  3 a shows SEM images of the 18Ni maraging steel in the as-built condition, highlighting the characteristic laser track pattern. In Fig.  3 b, after aging at 610 °C for 10 min, the original as-built microstructure is partially altered; faint outlines of the initial melt pools remain visible, while a typical lath martensitic structure begins to emerge. Figure  3 c displays the sample aged at 610 C for 30 min, where the martensitic microstructure is more pronounced. The 650 °C–10 min condition (Fig.  3 d) retains faint traces of cellular boundaries, like those observed after aging at 610 °C. However, the higher temperature promoted more extensive microstructural recovery, rendering the cellular array almost imperceptible at lower magnifications.

Fig. 3 Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of 18Ni maraging steel in ( a ) the as-built condition, and after aging at ( b ) 610 °C for 10 min, ( c ) 610 °C for 30 min, and ( d ) 650 °C for 10 min. All images were acquired on the build plane

sections.heading: X-ray diffraction
paragraphs: Figure  4  shows the X-ray diffractograms of analyzed samples. The As-built (AB) sample presents only BCC peaks, while both samples treated at 610 °C present BCC and FCC phases. The BCC corresponds to the martensitic phase, and the FCC corresponds to a fraction of reverted austenite formed during the aging treatment and kept stable during cooling until ambient temperature.
Fig. 4 X-ray diffractograms of the as built and heat-treated samples

On the other hand, the thermodynamic phases diagram (Fig.  5 ) shows that the sample treated at 650 °C has a higher austenite volume than 610 °C. Nonetheless, sample treated at 650 °C did not present FCC peaks, i.e., higher temperatures promote higher austenite reversion, but the most reverted austenite at 650 °C was transformed back to martensite upon cooling, this phenomenon has been reported iby some authors [ 13 ,  29 ,  30 ]. From Rietveld analysis in MAUD, phase quantification was performed, and the following austenite content (%) was calculated: 1.13, 7.83, 11.68, and 1.89% for AB, 610 °C–10 min, 610 °C–30 min and 650 °C–10 min respectively.

sections.heading: Thermodynamic analysis (thermo-calc)
paragraphs: To support microstructural characterization, the equilibrium phase diagram was simulated to predict the possible phase transformations near the aging temperatures. Figure  5  presents the thermodynamic diagram simulation of the phase fraction in function of temperature of a 18Ni maraging steel, accompanied by a single point temperature analysis depicting the phases in equilibrium and its chemical composition according to ThermoCalc software.
Fig. 5 Thermodynamic simulation: ( a ) 18Ni maraging phase fraction in function of temperature; ( b ) thermodynamic equilibria phases at 610 °C and 650 °C for 18Ni maraging steel

According to the diagram, it can be expected the formation of FCC (austenite), BCC (ferrite/martensite), Ni 3 Ti, Laves (Fe 2 Mo), and MU (Fe 7 Mo 6 ) phases depending on the target temperature of heat-treatment. Within the temperature range studied (610 °C to 650 °C), the MU (Fe 7 Mo 6 ) phase is not expected to occur unless its kinetics are sufficiently rapid to allow for the transformation of this phase during the cooling from higher temperatures to ambient temperature. For 610 °C, thermodynamic simulation predicts laves phase (Fe 2 Mo) and Ni 3 Ti formation, while for 650 °C, no indication of Ni 3 Ti was found according to Fig.  5 .

The BCC (martensite matrix) and FCC (austenite) phases are evident (Fig.  5 ). The BCC martensite forms due to high content of alloying elements, resulting in an athermal martensite, that is not influenced by the quenching medium or cooling rate. Because of the low carbon content, the crystal lattice experiences minimal distortion, leading to the formation of BCC martensite. Depending on the heat treatment time, the FCC phase can become enriched with gamma stabilizer elements [ 12 ,  13 ,  31 ], such as Ni and Co. What occurs is that diffusion-controlled process of segregation of austenite stabilizer elements is triggered when the steel is heated between Ac1 and Ac3. As time is prolonged, more elements such as Ni and Mn will segregate, producing a more stable austenite locally [ 12 ,  32 ]. As shown in Fig.  5 , the higher the temperature, the lower the Ni partitioning necessary to form austenite phase, having 24.7% Ni at 610 °C, and 20.8% Ni at 650 °C prediction. If enough time is provided, the Ni enrichment of austenite phase will enhance thermal stability, preserving it during cooling down to room temperature, resulting in a metastable phase known as reverted austenite [ 24 ,  33 ,  34 ]. It is noteworthy that reverted austenite was detected by XRD (Fig.  4 ) only in samples treated at 610 °C for 10 and 30 min, but not for 650 °C, even though thermodynamic simulation predicted the formation of 84.7% of austenite in the microstructure. This is specifically related to the austenite reversion and stabilization due to gamma stabilizers element enrichment, such as Ni.

The thermal stability of reverted austenite upon cooling is primarily governed by the degree of Ni partitioning. Experimental results confirm that the condition aged at 650 °C for 10 min exhibited negligible stabilization at room temperature observed by XRD data in Fig.  4 . As shown in the equilibrium thermodynamic diagram (Fig.  5 a), lower intercritical temperatures promote a more pronounced Ni enrichment within the FCC phase (γ eq ). Conversely, this chemical partitioning is significantly diluted as the equilibrium volume fraction of austenite increases with temperature. Consequently, at 650 °C, the Ni concentration in the austenite remains below the critical threshold required to depress the M S  temperature below room temperature, leading to a partial or total athermal transformation back into martensite during cooling.

Note that the concentration of Ni in a tempered condition at 650 °C is 20.8%, only 2% above the nominal composition. Supposing a resultant microstructure with 84.7% of austenite phase containing only 20.8% Ni concentration, this was not enough to cause thermal stability and preserve the austenite as a reverted austenite in room temperature. In the other hand, the 610 °C condition presented less austenite formation, which was expected, but with higher concentration of Ni (24.7%), which led to higher thermal stability and its presence after cooling according to the XRD collected data. Prolonging the 610 °C heat-treatment time will lead to convergence to this equilibrium austenitic volume value of 64.7% approximately. Thus, despite the equilibrium thermodynamic simulation indicating that a greater volume of austenite is generated at 650 °C compared to 610 °C, the sample treated at 650 °C did not show austenite XRD peaks (as observed in the diffractogram acquired at ambient temperature – Fig.  4 ).

sections.heading: Hardness
paragraphs: Figure  6  shows the Vickers microhardness measurements, these results evidence that aging treatments were effective to increase the hardness of material by precipitation of intermetallics. This effect of precipitation, even at higher temperatures such as 640 °C [ 14 ], has been extensively reported in the literature, not requiring TEM images to confirm [ 9 ,  16 ,  32 ,  35 ,  36 – 37 ].
Fig. 6 Vickers microhardness (HV 0.2 ) for the as built and heat-treated samples of 18Ni maraging steel

The hardness of as-built material was 361 ± 5 HV 0.2 , increasing especially in the conditions treated for 10 min. The sample treated at 650 °C for 10 min reached 554 ± 7 HV 0.2 , the one at 610 °C for 10 min achieved 540 ± 13 HV 0.2 , and the condition treated at 610 °C for 30 min attained 511 ± 7 HV 0.2 . Note that the hardness decreased in the condition treated at 610 °C when moving from 10 to 30 min of treatment (554 to 511 HV 0.2 ). Although it is not possible to observe through LOM and SEM images or XRD due to their size, this phenomenon is mainly attributed to the increased time (or temperature) allowing for the coarsening of intermetallics and subsequently related to further austenite reversion that enhances precipitate dissolution [ 16 ,  38 ,  39 – 40 ]. Precipitates go through the following steps: (i) formation of nuclei of the new phase; (ii) growth of these nuclei; (iii) coarsening of the precipitate without changing in its volume fraction [ 41 ,  42 ]. The first of these stages involves local clustering of the solute atoms to form what are commonly called Guinier-Preston or GP zones. These zones or clusters are favored by a low aging temperature, a small atomic size misfit, and a high degree of solute supersaturation [ 43 ]. Furthermore, precipitation does not begin immediately but requires a finite time before it is detectable. This time interval is called the incubation period and represents the time necessary to form stable visible nuclei. The speed at which precipitation occurs varies with temperature, which also dictates the maximum hardening effect. For higher temperatures, lower peak-hardness are achieved, and faster precipitation process occurs, leading faster to an overaged condition [ 41 ]. This was the case of prolonging aging from 10 to 30 min at 610 °C. The as-built condition experienced an increase in hardness after heat treatment at 610 °C for 10 min, due exclusively to precipitation hardening. However, extending the aging time from 10 to 30 min led to a decrease in hardness, indicating the onset of an overaged condition, which was also consequence of more austenite formation as seen in Fig.  4 . Condition 650 °C for 10 min presented the highest hardness, which is reasonable due to the lack of austenite formation. Additionally, as previously described, further aging at intercritical temperatures promotes austenite reversion. Initially, this transformation supports the precipitation process, but over time it begins to compete with it, leading to the dissolution of precipitates such as Ni 3 Ti, which contains Ni required for the austenite reversion process [ 44 ]. Although no nanoscale characterization techniques have been used to observe the occurrence of precipitation, morphology and the type of intermetallic compound, precipitation hardening is strongly suggested by the evolution of hardness and by reports in the literature [ 9 ,  16 ,  32 ,  35 ,  36 ,  37 ,  38 ,  39 ,  40 ,  41 – 42 ,  44 ].

sections.heading: Friction and wear behavior
paragraphs: Figure  7  shows typical results of coefficient of friction (CoF) as a function of test time. Two stages of friction behavior were identified, which was also valid for all tribological tests, after 6700 s. An initial transient behavior (running-in) exhibited high fluctuation of the CoF with a short period of continuous increment (up to approximately 500 s) followed by a steady-state regime.
Fig. 7 Coefficient of friction (CoF) obtained in the different tribological tests carried out

It is expected that during the running-in period, large plastic strains occur in the subsurface region [ 45 ], such that the friction work is mainly due to plastic deformation. During this period, the average chemical composition of the surface remains unchanged and severe wear caused by adhesive mechanisms is expected [ 46 ]. The severe wear causes the fast growth of the nominal contact area, and it is plausible that, at the end of this period, the plastic deformation component of the CoF is reduced when the nominal contact pressure reaches a threshold value [ 45 ].

The running-in period for all test conditions and test time occurred for t < 500 s, followed by the steady-state period with CoF approximately on the range 0.5 < µ < 0.7. It can be observed from Fig.  7  that the as-built sample exhibits the highest friction coefficient; samples treated at 610 °C (both treatment times) showed intermediate values while the condition treated at 650 °C presents the lowest friction coefficient.

Regarding the wear test, the mass loss was measured to investigate the amount of material removed by wear or gained by the oxidation effect. Figure  8  shows comparative values of wear rate measured after tribological tests for each test condition. It is observed that wear rate values are on the order of 10 − 9  to 10 − 10  [kg/N·m] (moderate). For the 610 °C–30 min test condition, an increase in the mass of the disk can be attributed to the formation of oxide films.
Fig. 8 Wear rate as a function of the test sample

Usually, higher hardness presents lower CoF and lower wear rate [ 47 ,  48 ,  49 ,  50 – 51 ]. In the present case, the sample 650 °C–10 min presented the highest hardness, the lowest CoF and lowest wear rate. Regarding the 610 °C for 10 and 30 min heat-treated conditions, similar hardness values were obtained, however, presenting different tribological response. In this discussion, the main feature that differentiated both conditions were the volume and stability of the reverted austenite. As discussed, lower times of reversion or higher temperatures lead to partial enrichment of the reverted austenite, causing lower thermal stability, and in many cases resulting in the transformation back to martensite [ 12 ,  13 ,  34 ]. Comparing a longer period of aging of 30 min against 10 min, a more thermal stable and coarse reverted austenite were produced. Literature shows that smaller austenites, and less enriched are more instable [ 52 ], allowing more plastic deformation [ 33 ], for example, other authors reported a comparison between a tempered 18Ni for 60 min leading to 11% elongation, contrasting with a tempered 18Ni steel for 30 min, leading to 16% elongation [ 9 ]. Therefore, the reverted austenite from 610 °C to 10 min presents less thermal stability promoting more plastic deformation. This plastic deformation was associated to higher accommodation of the counter-body, increasing the contact area of the ball with the 610 °C–10 min sample, decreasing wear rate but increasing CoF as observed in the data. Figure  7  clearly reveals a lower CoF of the 610 °C–10 min than the 610 °C–30 min in the earlier stages, but a gradual increase of the CoF of the 610 °C–10 min causes it to overcome the CoF value of the 610 °C–30 min in the middle of the steady-state near 3000 s. Sample 610 °C–30 min presented a more stable reverted austenite, which implied in lower plasticity when compared to the 610 °C–10 min, not presenting a gradual deformation, stabilizing the CoF and presenting a higher wear rate. Furthermore, the CoF observed in Fig.  7  all present a dry contact with oxidation shape curve [ 48 ]. However, observing Fig.  9 , can be seen that sample 610 °C–30 min presented a lower formation of oxides on its surface, which also contributed to a higher wear rate when compared to the other heat-treated samples.

sections.heading: Surface analysis
paragraphs: Upon reviewing the CoF and wear rate values obtained for the four testing conditions; it is evident that CoF decreases over time when transitioning from condition AB to the 650 °C–10 min condition. The wear rate, expressed in kg/Nm, indicates moderate wear and is characterized by a combination of wear mechanisms, including abrasion and adhesion. This observation is particularly noteworthy when evaluating each condition individually.

It was identified that for conditions AB (Fig.  9 a), 610 °C–10 min (Fig.  9 b), and 650 °C–10 min (Fig.  9 d) similar characteristics in the wear tracks, i.e., a wear mechanism associated with oxide formation, abrasion and adhesion.

Wear is a complex phenomenon typically encompassing mechanisms such as adhesion, abrasion, oxidative, fatigue cracking, or corrosion, which vary significantly between the running-in and steady-state stages. However, in this study, the primary mechanisms identified across all aged conditions were adhesive, oxidative and abrasive wear [ 28 ]. While fatigue and corrosion are recognized as possible wear modes in high-performance steels, no evidence of fatigue-induced cracking or corrosive degradation was observed under the specific sliding conditions tested here. It can observe in Fig.  9 c that sample 610 °C–30 min showed less oxide formation on the final wear surface among all samples. As the other conditions oxidized, it is much likely that the oxides formed on the 610 °C–30 min sample were adhered to the ball and contributed to the wear system, increasing wear rate. This can be related to a higher enrichment of the reverted austenite and depleting the Ni from the martensitic matrix, resulting in a heterogenous oxide more susceptible to detach. As-built condition presented oxide formation, and a surface morphology presenting many wear mechanisms, but mostly grooving and scratching of the oxide layer, presenting the appearance of a less brittle oxide layer. This contrasts with the Fig.  9 b and d 610 and 650 heat-treated for 10 min, which present a very dense oxide layer formation, observing mainly adhesion wear.
Fig. 9 Typical wear track after pin on disk tribological test for. ( a ) AB sample ( b ) 610 °C–10 min ( c ) 610 °C–30 min ( d ) 650 °C–10 min
Fig. 10 SEM images of wear track after pin on disk tribological tests for: ( a–b ) AB sample; ( c–d ) 650 °C–10 min sample

Figure  10  shows the comparative SEM images of worn surfaces obtained after 6,700 s at room temperature and dry sliding test condition for AB sample and 650 °C–10 min. Figure  10 b and d reveal the central region of the wear tracks from Fig.  10 a and c. This magnification reveals that the main wear mechanism an 18Ni maraging steel sample manufactured by LPBF technology depends on the posterior heat treatment, showing strong abrasion evidence for AB condition, with characteristic scratches in the slide direction, probably caused by a third body such as intermetallic or oxides (which is usually called debris), while a smoother surface is depicted in Fig.  10 c-d for 650 °C treated sample. Chemical traces of W and C were found at wear surfaces of all samples, found to be particles from the WC-Co wear pin, detected in the EDS analysis (Fig.  11 ). Furthermore, AB sample presents a clear plastic deformation, as shown in Fig.  10 b, and its higher plasticity surface is related to a much lower hardness compared to 650 °C–10 min condition.

In the case of 650 °C–10 min, less scratches are observed on its surface. As both AB and 650 °C–10 min sample presented negligible formation of austenite phase, the change of wear mechanism was due to hardness difference. In this case, the elevated hardness of 650 °C–10 min was due to intermetallic precipitation [ 14 ,  35 ]. The 650 °C–10 min sample apparently formed a more continuous surface oxide layer, as observed in Fig.  9 d, showing that the aging temperature effect on the material increases the development of a tribofilm, which contributed to decreasing the CoF. The wear tracks of the as-built (AB) and 650 °C–10 min samples reveal distinct degradation mechanisms. The AB surface is characterized by a central region featuring deep scratches induced by abrasive wear, likely caused by hard debris (WC-Co) originating from the pin material. In contrast, the 650 °C–10 min sample exhibits a smoother morphology dominated by oxidative wear, indicating the formation of a stable protective oxide layer [ 28 ]. The deposited material occupies the whole contact surface for the case of 650 °C–10 min as test condition with a higher quantity of material accumulated on the wear track (Fig.  9 d). This relevant alteration can explain the variation and the behavior of CoF and wear rates showed in Figs.  7  and  8  respectively.

sections.heading: Analyses of the oxide layer composition
paragraphs: Oxide films on pure iron, are formed below 570 °C at atmospheric pressure, and are composed of Fe 2 O 3  (hematite) on the outside surface and Fe 3 O 4  (magnetite) next to the Fe 2 O 3 . At temperatures above 570 °C, more stable FeO (wüstite) is formed in the inner region under the magnetite [ 53 ,  54 ].

EDS analyses of this tribofilm (dark layer in Fig.  11 ) were conducted on the disk tracks surfaces. Figure  11  indicates the presence of elements such as iron, cobalt, nickel, molybdenum and titanium, which are the constituent elements of the 18Ni maraging steel, but an intense peak of oxygen was also observed, which indicates oxidation.
Fig. 11 EDS analysis of adherent region on disk surface after tribological test for 650 °C–10 min sample

sections.heading: RAMAN spectroscopy analysis
paragraphs: Analyses by Raman spectroscopy were performed inside the wear track and Fig.  12  shows the Raman spectra for the studied conditions, Fe 3 O 4  (magnetite), Fe 2 O 3  (hematite), NiO (bunsenite), and (Ni 0.86 Fe 2+ 0.12 Co 0.01 )Fe 3+ 2 O 4  (trevorite).

The Raman peaks were not distinguishable for the as-built sample. This is addressed by a low hardness and high plasticity of the substrate, allowing severe plastic deformation, resulting in scratching, grooving and detaching of the formed oxides as observed in Fig.  10 . Sample 610 °C – 30 min presented the highest formation of NiFe₂O₄ trevorite spinel, suggested to be due to the highest formation of reverted austenite among the studied samples. This oxide has been reported in Fe-Ni compounds [ 55 ] and may have possibly formed due to reverted austenite, which segregates Ni content, presenting enriched regions with Ni with a stronger capacity to resist oxidation is promoted in the austenite regions at the surface. EDS in Fig.  11  proves Ni presence in the formed oxide, reinforcing the hypothesis of trevorite formation. This combination led to an intermittent oxide formation as observed Fig.  10 , not forming a sound and continuous oxide layer, but rather interleaved oxide/substrate. 610 °C–10 min and 650 °C–10 min presented moderate NiFe₂O₄ trevorite spinel formation of similar values between them. Furthermore, a strong formation of hematite was observed for 650 °C–10 min, which is likely to be due to a hard and almost fully martensitic substrate.

The wear characteristics of the surface oxide tribo-layers depend on the type of oxide formed on the sliding surface, as well as on the steel composition and test parameters, such as contact temperature and atmosphere. At low temperatures, the oxide layer is mainly composed of α-Fe 2 O 3 , which is removed from the wear track surface. At higher temperatures, a more compact layer with an increasing amount of Fe 3 O 4  contributes with the load-carrying support and wear resistance [ 56 ]. It is expected that during the friction of maraging steel, typical oxides such as FeO and Fe 2 O 3  will form. The formation of these oxides depends on the temperature reached during friction and the presence of oxygen. The formation of magnetite (Fe 3 O 4 ) is associated with the high temperatures (< 500 °C) and it is unlikely that it has formed, concluding that the peak at 700 cm − 1  is in fact trevorite [ 55 ].

Note that there is a direct relationship between the formation of oxides and the CoF (Fig.  7 ). The sample that showed the greatest formation of oxides presented the lowest CoF (650 °C–10 min), while the two conditions treated at 610 °C exhibit an intermediate friction coefficient. According to the hypothesis that the CoF is indirectly proportional to the greater formation of oxide, the as-built sample presented the highest CoF and would present the lowest oxide formation. In fact, and not distinguishable Raman peaks were found for AB sample, but Fig.  10  shows the presence of oxide in the wear track.

Fig. 12 Experimental Raman analysis inside the wear tracks after pin-on-disk tests: ( a ) samples Raman scattering; ( b ) typical Raman scattering of oxides – hematite, bunsenite, magnetite, NiFe₂O₄ trevorite spinel

Table  4  presents average data on the Mohs hardness and density of the oxides detected on the tracks after wear testing. Correlating this data with the CoF (Fig.  7 ) indicates a trend that harder oxides contribute to reducing the friction coefficient.

It can be observed that the highest CoF corresponds to the as-built material (Fig.  7 ), which also correlates with the lowest hardness and a relatively high wear rate (Fig.  8 ). This suggests the material is more ductile, resulting in greater plasticity during dry sliding. However, this condition is analyzed for comparative purposes, as it is not of technological interest since this material should be used in an aged condition.

Regarding the aged samples, the conditions 610 °C–10 min and 650 °C–10 min have similar hardness values and tribological behavior. Both samples presented high hardness and lowest wear rate among other conditions, statistically presenting the same wear rate. Also, similar wear mechanism is observed in Fig.  9 b and d, prevailing an oxidative wear [ 28 ] and the formation of a sound oxide layer. Small differences could be pointed, such as a higher average CoF for 610 °C–10 min sample (see Fig.  7 ), and more detaching of the oxide layer of sample 650 °C–10 min (Fig.  9 d) when compared to 610 °C–10 min (Fig.  9 b). This suggests that the oxides formed on the wear tracks of the 650 °C–10 min sample may be easier to flake off (Fig.  10 ). Furthermore, the 610 °C–10 min increase of CoF along wear testing, as well as higher CoF than 650 °C–10 min can be related to the presence of reverted austenite as a soft phase compared to the martensitic matrix. This could have led to plastic deformation beneath surface, resulting in a certain roughness that altered the CoF along the test [ 28 ].

Comparing the samples treated at 610 °C for different period times (10 and 30 min), it can be observed that a longer aging time results in microstructural changes that lead to a decrease in hardness, increase of austenite volume and a change in tribological behavior. Comparing 610 °C aged for 10 and 30 min, the treatment for 30 min resulted in a similar CoF, but the wear rate increased from 0.53 ± 0.35 to 1.98 ± 0.0 [kg/N·m]. As discussed in the XRD section, this is related to the content of reverted austenite, as this phase only appeared under 610 °C condition, with greater volume after 30 min of aging. It seems that the volume of the sample treated at 610 °C for 30 min is larger, which can be corroborated by the diffractograms in Fig.  4 , where this condition exhibits an austenite peak (111) that is not visible in the sample treated at 610 °C for 10 min. Moreover, the longer exposure of the sample during the aging treatment provides the necessary energy for increased precipitation and growth of intermetallics such as Ni 3 Ti and/or Laves (Fe 2 Mo) [ 40 ,  44 ].

sections.heading: Effect of reverted austenite on tribological behavior
paragraphs: The distinct thermal stability of the reverted austenite observed between the tested conditions is strongly governed by a competitive trade-off between chemical partitioning kinetics and phase growth morphology. At the lower aging temperature of 610 °C, the relatively low diffusion coefficient of nickel restricts its long-range migration, leading to a severe localized solute enrichment at the newly nucleated austenite embryos, particularly along lath boundaries and prior laser track interfaces. This high local Ni concentration drastically suppresses the martensite start temperature well below room temperature, chemically stabilizing the reverted austenite during subsequent cooling. This phenomena is observed in the Thermocalc simulations where at lower aging temperatures, more Ni is required to form austenite phase. Conversely, at 650 °C, the enhanced thermal energy accelerates long-range Ni diffusion while lower Ni is required to stabilize austenite phase compared to 610 °C condition, promoting a more rapid growth of the austenite phase and a consequent dilution of the solute content within a larger transformed volume. Because the average nickel content within this high-temperature austenite falls below the critical threshold required for chemical stabilization, the phase becomes thermally unstable and undergoes a re-transformation into fresh martensite upon cooling. Furthermore, the mechanical stability of the remaining austenite is directly compromised during sliding wear; under the severe shear stresses of the pin-on-disk test, this metastable phase undergoes a strain-induced martensitic transformation (TRIP effect), resulting in localized work hardening but simultaneously altering the surface plasticity and the adherence of the protective tribo-layer such as the formation of trevorite-rich layer.

The transition in the coefficient of friction and wear stability between the 610 °C and 650 °C conditions can be fundamentally explained by the mechanical interaction between oxide scale stability and substrate plasticity. The thin, rigid ceramic trevorite and other oxides formed in the oxide layer requires sufficient mechanical support from the underlying metallic matrix to withstand severe shear stresses during sliding. At 610 °C for 30 min, the substantial fraction of softer reverted austenite combined with overaging matrix softening decreases the substrate’s yield strength. Under loading, this induces severe localized plastic deformation in the subsurface region. Because the brittle oxide layer cannot accommodate the large plastic strains of the underlying substrate, it experiences mismatch stresses, leading to premature cracking and spallation. Once delaminated, these oxide fragments become trapped in the contact interface, which may act as abrasive debris (third-body effect) that plowed the wear track, which directly explains the higher CoF (0.60) and the descriptive scratches observed (Fig.  9 c). Conversely, the condition aged at 650 °C, containing a lower fraction of stable austenite and a re-transformed fresh martensite matrix, provides a more rigid substrate that effectively anchors the oxide scale, suppressing spallation and maintaining a steady, low friction behavior (0.50).

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Intercritical aging heat treatments were able to cause austenite reversion at 610 and 650 °C, and promote intermetallic precipitation to some extent, resulting in increased hardness compared to the as-built condition. Austenite reversion was up to 7.83, 11.68, and 1.89% for 610 °C for 10, 30 min and 650 °C for 10 min respectively. In terms of hardness, the conditions with aging treatment reached relatively similar values with an average of 532 HV 0.2 , which are higher than the as-built condition with 361 HV 0.2 . From the wear results it was possible to determine that the condition which exhibited the best performance, when comparing hardness values, friction coefficients, and wear rates, was that at 610 °C for 10 min. The as-built condition presented wear mechanism of grooving and scratching, presenting the appearance of higher surface plasticity. This was due to the lack of brittle mechanisms of failure, such as cracks and detaching of the oxide layer. This had resulted due to a very ductile substrate that enabled oxide to accommodate. Also, the continuous wear resulted in a indistinguishable Raman profile due to oxide deterioration. Contrasting, tempered samples presented a more brittle aspect, mainly those treated for 10 min (which also presented the highest hardness). High formation of NiFe₂O₄ trevorite spinel was found to be associated with content of reverted austenite.

All aged samples exhibited lower CoF values than the as-built condition, with wear rates on the order of 10 − 9  kg/Nm, characterizing a moderate wear regime dominated by adhesive, oxidative, and abrasive mechanisms. While the general trend of higher hardness correlating with enhanced wear resistance was confirmed with the 650 °C–10 min condition showing the best performance the role of reverted austenite proved to be a critical factor. The results indicate that unstable austenite fraction, as observed in the 610 °C conditions, leads to greater surface plasticity and lower mechanical support for the oxide layer. This instability promoted the premature detachment of the protective film (610 °C–30 min), subsequently increasing both the CoF and the wear rate compared to the more stable 650 °C–10 min condition.
